s15.slug: FRIDAY · 5:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL — A TABLE FOR A SAINT
body: The sun is low enough now to come straight down the lobby from the west doors, and the Fishbowl has gone gold in it, all four glass walls, so that from the mailboxes Jack can see the light in the room before he can see into it. Somebody has taped butcher paper across the lower half of the glass on the lobby side. It stops at about chin height. Over the top of it a row of heads he knows turns toward him at once, and Laney’s hand comes up and pulls Doug Pruitt’s head down out of sight, too late, and then her own.

Lena is outside the door, on the lobby side, with her back to the butcher paper. She’s in a blue dress with small white buttons he has never seen before, and an apron over it she has forgotten to take off, and her grandmother’s medal, and there is still a dusting of flour in the crook of one elbow. She looks him over once — the Carhartt, the flannel, the jeans he washes dishes in — and nods, a woman checking an item off a list.

body.text: She puts her hand on the push bar and doesn’t push it yet. “You’re going to cry,” she says. “I want you to.” She leans on the bar.
body.else: She puts her hand on the push bar and leans on it without a word.

body: The noise comes out at him — Laney’s “*Surprise!*” a little late, because everybody was waiting for somebody else to start; a whoop from Theo; Margot saying “Happy birthday” at an ordinary speaking volume — and under it Louis Prima, out of Theo’s iPhone, which is standing in a coffee mug on a side table for a speaker, so that the song comes out of the mug sounding like it’s being sung up from the bottom of a well in Naples. The couches have been shoved back against the windows. The broken foosball table is up against the wall under a bedsheet, and there is something rectangular under the sheet that nobody is looking at. He knows two-thirds of the people in here and has been introduced to the rest.

He doesn’t want a fuss. Everybody in this room knows it; it’s possible that’s why there are so many of them. He stands just inside the door with his hands in the Carhartt’s pockets and takes them out again, because Nonna would have them off at the wrist, and nods at people with his father’s wake nod, chin down and up. Kevin lifts a paper plate at him. Peter Haddad from Newman, whom he knows mostly from announcements, is filming on a Canon the size of a deck of cards. He says, “You guys,” which is not a sentence, and Lena, behind him, puts two fingers in the small of his back and steers him in.

The altar is against the long wall where the TV usually lives, and it goes up in three steps nearly to the ceiling tiles. There are milk crates under it — he can see a blue one where a cloth doesn’t quite reach the carpet — and across the top tier a door, a real door, six panels and the hole for the knob, off its hinges from somewhere in the basement. Three white tablecloths over everything, three slightly different whites. “One from every dining hall on this campus,” Laney announces to the room, “and every one goes back Monday morning, so if you spill, you are dead to me.”
“Three tiers,” Lena is telling an RA with a lanyard, “one for each Person of the Trinity. And the saint goes at the top, where he’d be most embarrassed.”

body.text: At the top, between two votives in red glass, in a brass frame he has never seen, is a holy card with its corners worn soft as cloth: Saint Joseph with the lilies and the Child and the carpenter’s square, *PRIEZ POUR NOUS*. He knows it before he’s halfway across the room. It lives on the ledge over his bed in 412, propped against the wall by his alarm clock, and he hasn’t looked at the ledge since Thursday. Across the room Theo is adjusting the coffee mug a little to the left, very precisely.
body.else: At the top, between two votives in red glass, in a brass frame he has never seen, is a holy card from the rack on the Newman table: Saint Joseph with the lilies and the Child and the carpenter’s square, propped up like a portrait over a mantel.

body: There are white lilies on every tier, in Albertsons cellophane with the price stickers turned to the wall. “He gets lilies,” Lena tells the RA. “It’s his whole look.”

The breads are on the middle tier, and he has to stand in front of them and read them, because they are bread and they are also things. A long loaf with dough flowers bunched at the top: the staff. A braid: the beard. Two flat soles with the straps scored in: sandals. A hammer. A cross. Two in the back row came out dark as a saddle at one end, and he knows exactly which side of Rudy’s oven they were on. And in front, dead center, where you would put the thing you were proudest of, there is a loaf in the shape of the state of Ohio.

It is unmistakably Ohio. The lake ragged along the top, the river scalloping the bottom, the two straight sides where Indiana and Pennsylvania begin. Up in the right-hand corner, about where Youngstown is, somebody has pricked one hole with a toothpick. That’s what does it. Not the door off the basement, not the lilies, not the room full of people with plates. A hole the size of a pencil point in a piece of bread, put there by somebody who looked it up.
“That’s Ohio,” Lena tells the floor, not him. “The hole is Youngstown. Rudy wanted to do Cleveland too, and I told him nobody asked for Cleveland.”

He has to look at the fava beans for some time after that. They are in a cut-glass bowl that must belong to the Newman Center, brown and flat and dry, Nonna’s, out of a shoebox from Glenwood Avenue. Beside them, Celeste’s cuccidati in the blue Royal Dansk tin from Dupre Street, with the lid propped against it. Zeppole, Nonna’s kind, the cream piped in and a candied cherry pressed into every one. Lemons and oranges heaped on all three tiers. A dozen stuffed artichokes packed with crumbs and garlic. A foil pan of spaghetti under a drift of toasted breadcrumbs, and Margot, passing behind him with a plate, says, “The breadcrumbs represent sawdust, because he was a carpenter, and I checked three sources and every one of them said so with a straight face,” and keeps going. The lagane e ceci, wide noodles and chickpeas, Nonna’s, carried out here through two telephones. Rudy’s fish, whole and fried gold, on a platter with its mouth open as if it has something to say about the oven.

body.text: And on the bottom tier, among the lemons, a bottle of Barq’s, unopened, standing with its label turned out. He knows that bottle. Lena is explaining the Trinity to a sophomore, and does not look at him while he looks at it.

body: None of it has been within a mile of a cow. “It was a Lenten table before it was a feast,” Lena tells Doug Pruitt, who wanted to know why the fish has a face, “and you don’t change a recipe on a saint.”

On the side table, beside Theo’s coffee mug, there is a stockpot from the Anchor with its lid on, and a ladle laid across a saucer. Lena has stood a folding chair in front of it, like a velvet rope at a museum.

Father Osei comes in from the lobby at a quarter to six with his stole in his coat pocket and a Smucker’s jar of holy water with the label soaked off, and the room gets quieter without anyone deciding to. He kisses the stole and puts it on over his sweater. He blesses in Latin first, the old grace — *Benedic, Domine, nos et haec tua dona* — unhurried, and then in English, in his own words: this table and the hands that made it; the bread and the beans and the fish; the poor who will eat from it tomorrow; all fathers — and there his voice does one small thing, and goes on — and this young man, on his feast. He shakes the water off his fingers over the three tiers, and it patters on the cellophane, and some of it lands on Jack. Jack notices only that he looks at the card at the top a moment longer than he looked at the bread. He wets his fingers again and blesses the bowl of beans by itself.
“The *tupa tupa*!” Laney claps twice, in a voice built for a stadium. “Places. Jack, you’re Joseph, Lena, you’re Mary, y’all go out in the lobby and knock —”
“Absolutely not,” Lena says.

That’s all she says. Laney looks across the altar at Theo, over the lilies, and Theo looks back at her. It lasts as long as it takes a votive to gutter and stand up straight again. Theo goes back to the coffee mug and Laney to her clipboard, and as far as Jack can tell he is the only person in the Fishbowl who saw it.

So Margot is Joseph. She has a mop handle out of the second-floor janitor’s closet for a staff, with a lily duct-taped to the top, and she holds it like a halberd. “I’ve done the reading,” she says, to nobody in particular. Laney is Mary, in the blue shower curtain off the fourth-floor bathroom, worn as a mantle and safety-pinned at the throat: hips back, chin up, a hand at her heart. In the crook of her arm, swaddled in a dish towel, is Coco the coconut, the Bambino for the evening, looking up at the ceiling tiles with a perfectly serene Sharpie face. They process out to the lobby. They knock on the glass.
Theo, inside, an apron over his cashmere and a dish towel on his arm, opens the door a crack. “No room. There’s a convention. Orthodontists.” He shuts it.

Laney knocks again, harder, and Coco nearly goes. Theo opens it another crack. “Still no room. I’ve read this one. A couple, a donkey, no reservation. Every studio in town passed. Nobody is financing a period piece in this economy.” He shuts it.

The third knock comes while Theo has gone back to fix the music. Kevin is standing by the door with an empty plate he hasn’t been allowed to fill, and he opens it, mildly, because somebody is knocking. Laney sails in past him, then turns round and takes him by the elbow too, and steers him to the card table where the saints are to be fed first — Margot, and herself, and Coco in her towel.
“Laney. I opened a door.”
“Because the brokenhearted count, sugar.” She sits him down. And he lets her.

After the saints, everybody, standing, off paper plates. The walls are glass, and people going by in the lobby slow down, and look in, and are waved inside: a kid from Ferrer with a skateboard under his arm, who eats three zeppole one after another and says “Dude” softly to each of them; two RAs; Marcus from the desk, who has put a sign on the desk bell and stands by the window with a plate of fish, having signed for half of this table this week and wanting to see how it came out; a tall girl from the Newman band. Gloria and Rudy are at the end of the table. Gloria has her coat on and something beside her under a dish towel that she has told three separate people not to touch. Rudy is watching people eat his fish, and nods every time somebody takes from the head end.

People keep coming up to say happy birthday, and Jack keeps saying thanks, and at some point it stops being something he has to get through. He eats a zeppola in two bites and gets cream on the Carhartt. He eats an artichoke leaf by leaf, standing by the window with Kevin, who explains the anatomy of an artichoke heart for a test Jack is apparently going to have on it. He is laughing at something Theo has said about the fish when Lena takes him by the sleeve and walks him to the side table, and moves the folding chair, and lifts the lid off the stockpot.

He knows it by the smell before he looks. Escarole, and the broth, and the Parmesan, and under it whatever it is his mother does that nobody else does: the kitchen on Glenwood on any Sunday in winter, with the windows steamed. He looks. The escarole gone dark and soft, the acini di pepe, the meatballs the size of marbles — the size Ma rolls them between her palms, a hundred at a time, with the phone in the crook of her neck.
Meat. On a Friday. In Lent.

He looks at her. Lena Broussard has not eaten meat on a Friday in Lent since she was old enough to be told why. On Dupre Street the altar is meatless and so is the house — shrimp, crawfish, red beans without the ham — and he knows it as well as he knows her handwriting.
“It’s a solemnity,” she says. “The Church says I may.” She lets it stand long enough for him to hear the rest coming. “It doesn’t say I have to.”
She ladles two of the Commons’ waxed-paper coffee cups full, and hands him one, and lifts hers.
“That’s how much I like you, Costigan.”

Then she fishes out a meatball with a plastic spoon and eats it, solemnly, like a woman taking an oath, with her eyes on his — and her face betrays her. It’s good. It’s much too good. She makes a face at it, scandalized, as though the soup has cheated.

choices.key: At the St. Joseph altar Lena built for your birthday, you tasted your mother’s wedding soup and told her it tasted like home.
response: “Your mother said you’d say that,” Lena says. “She said if you didn’t, I’d used the wrong escarole.”

He drinks, and it isn’t the wrong escarole. It’s Ma’s, down to the pepper she puts in when nobody’s watching. Before he’s finished, Lena takes the cup out of his hand and fills it again from the pot, as she would in her own kitchen for somebody home from school who hasn’t eaten.

choices.text: “Nobody’s done this since my brother went away.”
choices.key: At the St. Joseph altar Lena built for your birthday, you told her nobody had done this since your brother went away.
response: “I know,” she says. “That’s why I did it.”

She doesn’t make it any bigger than that. She puts her hand on his sleeve, on the canvas at his wrist, in front of Theo and the Ferrer kid and Marcus from the desk and everybody with a paper plate, and leaves it there for about as long as a Glory Be, and takes it back, and picks up her soup.

choices.text: “You ate meat on a Friday. For me. I’m telling Mémère.”
choices.key: At the St. Joseph altar Lena built for your birthday, you threatened to tell her grandmother she’d eaten meat on a Friday.
response: “Mémère *told* me to. On the phone, Wednesday. She said a saint’s day is a saint’s day and the boy is too thin.”
She eats another meatball at him, deliberately, holding his eye while she chews, chin up — defiant about it, and delighted about it, and plainly not stopping till the cup is empty.

s16.slug: FRIDAY · 6:15 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — TRUMBULL
body: The RAZR goes off against his ribs in the middle of a cuccidato. He feels it before he hears it; you couldn’t hear a smoke alarm in the Fishbowl. On the little outside screen, the long 330 number he has never saved and never needed to.

He is out through the lobby and into the east stairwell by the third ring, and up the first half flight, where he sits down on the turn with the concrete cold through his jeans and the party shrinks to Louis Prima and thirty people coming up through the floor. He opens the phone. The recorded woman runs through her paragraph — prepaid, Trumbull Correctional, monitored and recorded — with his brother’s name dropped into the hole in the middle of it in his brother’s own voice. He presses one.
“*Professor.*”

Danny doesn’t wait for hello. He sings. He gets as far as *Happy birthday* in a voice like a garbage disposal with a spoon in it, and somebody on the block behind him yells something that doesn’t make it through the line, and Danny says, off the phone, “It’s my *brother’s* birthday, Reggie, have a little *class*,” and Jack is laughing on the step with his forehead on his knee.
“Nineteen,” Danny says, and coughs. “You feel old?”
“I feel nineteen.”
“That’s the trouble with it.” A television behind him, a game, a whistle, men groaning at a call. “Ma says the veil girl’s doing a table.”
“She did it.”
“She *did* it.” Danny says it slow, like he’s writing it on the wall. “So? What’d she do?”

And Jack tells him, the short version: the three tiers and the door off the basement, the lilies, the bread like Ohio with the hole in it, the fish, Laney marching a coconut out to the lobby to knock on the glass. Danny interrupts once. “There’s a cake?”
“There’s something under a sheet on the foosball table that everybody’s pretending isn’t there.”
“Under a *sheet*. Like a body.” He’s delighted. “Go on.” And when Jack has gone on, to the end, Danny says, “Who played Joseph?”
“Margot.”
“Who’s Margot?”
“You’d like her. She has footnotes.”

Danny laughs. It’s the big one, the one that gets away from him and goes on and turns into the cough at the end, and somebody on his end tells him to keep it down, and he doesn’t. And then, still laughing, lighter than anything: “That was always me. You were the baby.” And straight on, without a breath: “Hey — the C.O. finished it. The book. Took him since October. Still says it’s about a house. I says, it’s about a *family*, Officer, and he says, Costigan, what do you think a house is.”
Jack sits on the step with the phone against his ear, and the line goes past him the way a car goes past a man on a curb.

Reggie, Danny reports, has taken up crochet for the arthritis in his hands and is making Danny a hat in wine and gold whether Danny wants one or not, and measured Danny’s head for it with a shoelace while he was asleep. There’s a new guy on the block from Akron who cries at Cavs games, actual tears, a grown man with a neck tattoo. The Cavs keep winning, and Danny refuses to discuss it in case it hears him. The food is the food. Ma sounded good Wednesday. Pop even got on the phone.
“You smoking?”
“Lent.”
“Good.”

The pack is where it has been since Ash Wednesday, in the breast pocket of the Carhartt: Marlboro Reds, the cellophane still on, day thirty-one. He can smell them through it, or thinks he can. It’s a solemnity. It’s his birthday. There is a priest in the next room who would at least hear the argument out. He puts his hand over the pocket, feels the hard corner of the box through the canvas, and takes the hand away.

Below him the lobby door opens and Lena comes through sideways with a paper plate in each hand, a cuccidato on each, and sees the phone, and stops at the foot of the flight. She doesn’t come any farther.

choices.key: When Danny called from Trumbull on your birthday, you handed Lena the phone so she could tell him about the table.

response.text: He holds it out to her. She sets the plates on the bottom step and comes up to the turn and takes the phone in both hands. “Danny? It’s Lena.” “The veil girl,” Danny says, loud enough that Jack can hear it from where he sits.
response.else: He holds it out to her. She sets the plates on the bottom step and comes up to the turn and takes the phone in both hands. “Hello?” “Who’s this?” Danny says, loud enough that Jack can hear it from where he sits. “Lena.” “*The* Lena.”

response: And she tells him what was on the table — all of it, in order, the way she’d tell a parish what the fish fry cleared: the tiers and why there are three, the staff and the beard and the sandals, the two loaves Rudy’s oven ruined, Ohio, the fish, the beans out of Nonna’s own shoebox, her mother’s fig cookies. At the zeppole Danny stops her. “Nonna’s?” Jack hears him say, small through the speaker. “Nonna’s,” Lena says. “Your mother read them to me over the phone, and Nonna corrected her twice.” There’s a pause from Trumbull, and when it comes it’s Danny to her, not to him: “Thanks for doing it. Somebody ought to.”

The recording breaks in over whatever she was going to say back — one minute — and she gives Jack the phone without a word. He gets ten seconds. “Love you, Professor. Happy birthday.” After that there’s no hallway in his ear anymore, no game, no Reggie: only the stairwell. Lena has gone down for the plates and come back, and is sitting on the step below his with her back against the rail, a paper plate on each knee.

choices.text: “She did the whole thing, D. Nonna’s table. In a dorm.”
choices.key: When Danny called from Trumbull on your birthday, you told him Lena had done Nonna’s whole table, in a dorm.
response: On the line Danny says, “*Good.*”

Nothing, for the length of a free throw, but the game on the television behind him and one long breath going out of him somewhere in Trumbull County. It is the closest Danny comes. A tone cuts in, and the recorded woman, flat as a bus schedule, says there is one minute remaining. “Love you, Professor. Happy birthday.” And the line is simply gone, mid-whistle.
Lena comes up the flight with the plates and sits down beside him on his step, close, and hands him one, and eats her cookie, and looks at the cinderblock wall with him, which tonight is the view.

choices.text: *Keep him to yourself for the fifteen minutes.*
choices.key: When Danny called from Trumbull on your birthday, you kept him to yourself for all fifteen minutes.
response: He lifts one finger to her over the rail. She nods.

So he and Danny talk about nothing. The Cavs, who are not to be discussed. Reggie’s hat. The weather in Leavittsburg: sleet. “God sends it to Trumbull County special, Professor, it ain’t sleet anywhere else in Ohio” — Whether Pop has fixed the storm door yet. He hasn’t. Nothing at all, for twelve more minutes, and it is the best part of the day, and he would not trade it for the altar. The warning comes in like a hand on his shoulder. “Love you, Professor. Happy birthday.” And then just the stairwell, and the party downstairs.
He looks down. Lena is at the foot of the flight where she has been all along, and when he looks she holds a plate up to him at arm’s length, a cuccidato on it.

s16a.slug: FRIDAY · 7:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL — THE LUCKY BEAN
body: The sun has gone behind the hills, and the glass walls have turned to mirrors, so that the Fishbowl looks twice its size and has two altars in it, the real one and its reflection standing out over the dark lawn. The real one is two-thirds gone. Father Osei left at seven with a plate under foil for the rectory and a lemon in each coat pocket. The Ferrer kid is asleep in an armchair with his skateboard on his chest.

Laney whips the sheet off the foosball table. Under it is a Texas sheet cake in a pan nearly as big as the table, chocolate, with pecans all over the top and nineteen candles set in it in what might be the shape of a 19. Lena exiled it there at five o’clock. (“It’s *cake*, Laney, not a sacramental.”) Laney drops a sash over Jack’s head — white satin, rhinestones, BIRTHDAY BOY — and settles it across the Carhartt from shoulder to hip, and steps back to judge it, and the room sings at him in four keys, Margot half a beat behind everybody on purpose. He blows the candles out in two tries, and is given a corner piece, because the birthday boy gets a corner, Laney says; it’s in the Constitution. Lena is by the lilies with her arms folded, singing louder than anyone, and flat.

Then the presents, which he was told there wouldn’t be. From Kevin, a box of medical-grade nitrile gloves, size large, for the Hobart: “For the maceration.” From Theo, a one-sheet of *Rocky* in a black frame: “The most Catholic film ever made, Costigan. The first thing you see is Jesus over the ring, and the last word is a girl’s name.” From Margot, an index card, typed, handed over face down. From Gloria, the thing under the dish towel, a coconut cream pie, set into his hands — “Don’t argue with me” — and from Rudy a handshake like a bench vise. From Father Osei, the holy card he left on the arm of the couch: Joseph with a sheaf of wheat, *Ite ad Ioseph*, which he explained at the door on his way out, in one sentence and a laugh — Pharaoh said it to the hungry, about the other Joseph, and it has never stopped being good advice.

body.title: An index card, typed
body.text: FIELD NOTE. St. Joseph is patron of workers, fathers, the dying, the Universal Church, and people trying to sell a house. You are at least two of these. —M.L.

body: On the couch Laney is reading his Facebook wall to Lena off her BlackBerry, because Lena gave up Facebook for Lent and is not allowed to look, and has her eyes shut to prove it: twenty-three people, his old CYO coach, and Becca Lindell, *birthdays count for a week at our house!!*, which Laney reads out with both exclamation points.
Lena brought his mail down from the desk at four and kept it, and hands it to him now. A big envelope from Glenwood Avenue in his mother’s writing, with a sheet of construction paper folded inside:

body.title: A drawing in crayon, from Glenwood Avenue
body.text: THIS IS JOSEPH. (St. Joseph, with a hammer and a carpenter’s square. At the bottom, unexplained, a crab.)

body: He studies the crab, and decides he will never ask Rosie about the crab as long as he lives.

And a small square envelope postmarked Breaux Bridge, with a card inside: a Joseph on the front in a printed gold frame, and pencil inside, an old woman’s pencil. Lena takes it out of his hands while he’s still working at the flap, and reads him one line, Mémère’s French in her mouth — “*Bonne fête au garçon de l’Ohio*” — and closes it, and puts it in her jean jacket. “For later.”

Last, she takes a bean from the bowl, one of Nonna’s, brown and flat, blessed with the rest of them at half past five, and holds out her other hand to him, palm up, for his wallet. He gives it to her.
“Keep one of these on you and you’re never broke a day,” she says. “Nonna’s orders. The Sicilians’ too.”

choices.text: “I’m a dishwasher. You’re going to need more beans.”
response: “It’s a *bean*, Youngstown, not a stimulus package.”
She tucks it in behind his driver’s license, where the State of Ohio can keep an eye on it, and hands the wallet back with a little slap into his palm. Paid in full.

choices.text: *Let her do it. Watch her do it.*
response: She does it carefully, as though the wallet were a missal: past his four dollars and his library card and the folded paper with the Glenwood numbers on it that he has never needed, until she finds the place behind his license, and slides the bean in there, and smooths the leather down over it with her thumb.
She gives it back to him. Her hand rests on top of the wallet, on top of his hand, and then it comes away.

choices.text: “Nonna mailed these to you, not me.”
response: “She did. I’m a bean courier now. It’s a very old order.”

She puts his bean behind his license. She takes a second one out of the bowl and drops it into the breast pocket of her own jean jacket, and buttons the pocket over it, looking at him while she does it.

s17.slug: FRIDAY · 11:48 PM · DELGADO HALL, HER LANDING — LE 19 MARS
body: Twelve minutes left of the nineteenth, by the RAZR lying open on the step. The building has gone quiet at last; somewhere above them a shower runs, and stops. The window on her landing is black glass with the stairwell in it — the tube light, the fire door, the two of them.

They came up at half past ten, when the Fishbowl was down to Laney asleep on a couch in her shower curtain and Kevin and Margot stacking the folding chairs, and Lena said she wanted to sit somewhere that didn’t smell of fish.

She’s on her step with her back to the cinderblock, in the jean jacket over a sweater, and socks: red wool ones, darned at one heel. The white ones are in her drawer. He is on the step below, sideways, the BIRTHDAY BOY sash rolled up beside him like a bandage, with a slab of Laney’s cake on a napkin that neither of them has touched since half past ten.

She takes Mémère’s card out of her jacket and opens it on her knee. She reads him the line again — “*Bonne fête au garçon de l’Ohio*” — and then the rest, in English, a sentence at a time, the pencil going up and down hill across the card, in something close to Mémère’s own voice, dry and level, a voice that has outlived most of the people who ever argued with it: “Happy birthday to the boy from Ohio. It is the day of Saint Joseph also, so you must share it, and he was here first. You were a good boy in my house but too thin. Eat what is put in front of you. Come back when the crawfish are fat. Odile Broussard.” She turns it to the light. “And then she drew a cross under her name, which means she’s praying for you, or that she doesn’t trust the post office. With her it’s both.”

body.text: She doesn’t put the card away. “On Ash Wednesday,” she says, “in the front room. She held on to that holy card with you and talked at you for a minute and a half, and I stood in the door and told you she said Joseph was a good man.”
body.else: She doesn’t put the card away. “She told me on the phone in February what she thought about Joseph,” she says. “I never passed it on.”

body: “She said Joseph doesn’t say one word. Not in all four Gospels. Not one. He has a dream and he gets up and does what he’s told, and that’s all we ever get out of him. And God trusted him with everything anyway. The girl, and the baby.” She looks at the card on her knee. “She said a man who can wait is worth ten who can talk. And then she said *that one*” — and Lena lifts her chin at him, from her step, as Mémère must have from the daybed — “*that one waits like a man who’s had practice.*”

body.text: “I didn’t translate that part,” Lena says. “I was holding a sweater.”
body.else: “I didn’t pass that part on,” Lena says. “I didn’t know what you’d do with it.”

body: He sits with that. Since August, every step of it, and an old woman in Breaux Bridge had it figured before he did.
He asks it now, finally. “Who told her?”
“I did.”

She says it to the card first, and then she looks up and says the rest to him. “At Christmas. On the phone to Breaux Bridge, the week I was deciding things.” She doesn’t say what things. He was in Youngstown that week, carrying his phone from room to room. “She asked me who I was thinking about so hard I’d let the roux burn, and I told her your birthday instead of your name. It was the only thing about you I could say out loud.”

He doesn’t have anything to say to that. He reaches up and takes the hand that isn’t holding the card, and she gives it to him, and they sit that way, his elbow on her step, her fingers cold from the stairwell.

body.text: Brisk now, putting the card back in her jacket: “I’ll have you know this was very hard.” “The soup?” “*All* of it. Your grandmother writes in a code. Rudy’s oven is a liar. Laney wanted a *fog machine*.”
Brisk now, putting the card back in her jacket: “I’ve been thinking about the soup since Monday.” His own words, returned with the socks attached.
Brisk now, putting the card back in her jacket: “It cost a great deal more than five dollars.”
She puts the card back in her jacket and doesn’t say anything about the soup, or the oven, or any of it.

body: The phone on the step says 11:58 when she leans down off her step and kisses him.

It isn’t quick, and it isn’t in a hurry to become anything else. Both her hands come flat against his chest, on the canvas, the way she stopped him by the Hobart, and he waits for them to push — and they don’t; they stay, and press, and keep him exactly where she wants him. His hand goes into the hair at the back of her head, still stiff in one place with flour she missed, and the other settles at her waist, over the sweater, and stays there. She tastes of anise and coffee and Laney’s frosting. He wants her — the weight of her leaning down to him, the warmth coming through the wool, the small sound she makes when he tips her head back — and what he notices, under all of it, is the order it comes in. Her first. The girl who called his mother on Monday; the bread with the hole in it; the hands that didn’t push. Then the wanting, after her, where it belongs, glad to be there. His hands stay where they are, and he doesn’t have to make them.
The phone turns over to 12:00. She sits back on her step, her hands still where they were, and her hair is a ruin, and she has never looked so pleased with herself.
“It’s not your birthday anymore,” she says. “I don’t kiss commoners.”

choices.text: “Best birthday I’ve had since I was a kid.”
choices.key: When your birthday ended on her landing, you told Lena it was the best one you’d had since you were a kid.
response: She doesn’t make a joke of it. She looks at him from her step for as long as it takes the tube light to flicker and steady.
“Good,” she says.

She takes her hands back and gets up and goes down the half flight to two in her red socks. At the wired glass she turns round with the door half open and looks up at him, and whatever she was going to say, she keeps. Through the wire in the glass he watches her go down the hall, past Margot’s door and the bulletin board, and stop at 217 and lift Mémère’s card at him, the length of the corridor away.

choices.key: When your birthday ended on her landing, you reminded Lena who you’d been with at Christmas, and she said she’d told her grandmother your birthday anyway.
response: “I know who you were with,” Lena says. “I told her anyway.”
It isn’t a reproach. It’s a fact she has kept since December, and she hands it to him level and by the edges, like a hot plate.
She had started to get up. She sits back down on her step instead, and pulls the red socks up over her heels, and settles her back against the cinderblock for one more minute of Saturday.

choices.key: When your birthday ended on her landing, you said nothing and let it be Saturday.
response: They sit. The building ticks somewhere in its pipes. After a while she lays her head on his shoulder, on the Carhartt, and leaves it there long enough for the RAZR’s little screen to give up and go dark on the step.

She gets up at last, and going past him she touches the top of his head, lightly, testing a loaf, and goes down the half flight. At the bottom, in her red socks, with the door to two already open, she lifts one hand without turning round.
